q: Which scientist first discovered the magnetic effect of electric current (in 1820)?
e: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted discovered that electric current in a wire deflects a nearby compass needle.

q: What is the direction of magnetic field lines OUTSIDE a bar magnet? (JAC 2024)
o: From South pole to North pole
From North pole to South pole
e: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines emerge from the North pole and merge into the South pole.

q: An electric motor converts which form of energy into which form? (JAC 2020)
e: An electric motor is a rotating device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

q: An electric generator converts which form of energy into which form? (JAC 2026)
e: An electric generator works on electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.

q: Which is the most important safety method used for protecting home appliances from short-circuiting or overloading? (JAC 2025 / NCERT)
e: Per NCERT, an electric fuse is the single most vital safety device protecting circuits against overloading and short-circuiting.

q: What are the standard voltage and frequency of domestic AC power supply in India?
e: In India, domestic AC mains operate at 220 V potential difference and 50 Hz frequency.

q: After every how many seconds does domestic AC in India (50 Hz) reverse its direction? (NCERT / JAC 2025)
e: At 50 Hz, there are 50 cycles/s; since direction reverses twice per cycle (100 times/s), each reversal takes 1/100 s.

q: What are the standard insulation colours for Live, Neutral, and Earth wires in household wiring (per NCERT)?
e: Per NCERT convention: Red = live wire, Black = neutral wire, and Green = earth wire.

q: What is the nature of the magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid carrying electric current? (NCERT)
o: Is uniform (the same) at all points inside
e: Parallel equally-spaced field lines inside a long solenoid show that the magnetic field is uniform throughout its interior.

q: Who discovered the phenomenon of electromagnetic induction (in 1831)?
e: Michael Faraday discovered in 1831 that changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an electric current.

q: What is the S.I. unit of magnetic field strength?
e: The S.I. unit of magnetic field strength is the tesla (T), named after Nikola Tesla.

q: What is the direction of magnetic field lines INSIDE a bar magnet?
o: From South pole to North pole
e: Magnetic field lines form closed loops—flowing N to S outside the magnet and returning S to N inside.

q: In Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, what do the forefinger, middle finger, and thumb represent respectively? (JAC 2020)
e: In Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (motors): Forefinger = Field, Middle finger = Current, Thumb = Force/Motion.

q: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule is used to find the direction of:
o: Induced electric current in a conductor moving in a magnetic field (generator rule)
e: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule gives the direction of induced current when a conductor moves across magnetic field lines.

q: Which rule gives the direction of magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying conductor?
e: Right-Hand Thumb Rule: point the right thumb along the current; curled fingers show the circular magnetic field direction.

q: The end of a current-carrying solenoid at which the current appears to flow anticlockwise behaves as which magnetic pole? (JAC 2026)
e: By the Clock Face Rule, anticlockwise current produces a North pole, whereas clockwise current produces a South pole.

q: Which instrument detects the presence and direction of even tiny electric currents in a circuit?
e: A galvanometer detects small currents and indicates their direction via left/right deflection from a central zero.

q: Which core material is used inside a coil to construct a strong temporary electromagnet?
e: Soft iron magnetises strongly when current flows and loses magnetism quickly when switched off—ideal for electromagnets.

q: Which material placed inside a current-carrying solenoid retains magnetism to form a permanent magnet?
e: Hard steel retains its induced magnetisation permanently after current is turned off.

q: What is the role of the split-ring commutator in a DC electric motor?
o: Reverse the direction of current in the armature coil after every half rotation
e: The split ring reverses coil current every half turn so torque continues pushing rotation in the same direction.

q: What is the essential structural difference between an AC generator and a DC generator? (NCERT)
o: AC uses electromagnet; DC uses permanent magnet
AC generator uses slip rings whereas DC generator uses a split-ring commutator
e: An AC generator employs two slip rings, while a DC generator uses a split-ring commutator.

q: What is the pattern of magnetic field lines around a straight conductor carrying current?
o: Concentric circles centred on the wire
e: Magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire form concentric circles around the wire.

q: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect each other? (NCERT)
o: At a point of intersection, a compass needle would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is impossible
They only exist in straight lines
e: If two field lines crossed, a compass placed there would point in two directions at once—physically impossible.

q: How is a uniform magnetic field represented graphically by field lines?
o: By parallel, equally spaced straight lines
By diverging rays from a point
e: Parallel and equidistant straight lines indicate uniform magnetic field strength and direction.

q: Which pair correctly gives one source of Direct Current (DC) and one source of Alternating Current (AC)?
o: DC: power grid; AC: dry cell
DC: battery / dry cell; AC: AC generator / domestic power mains
Both come only from solar cells
e: Cells/batteries supply DC, whereas household wall sockets fed by power station generators supply AC.

q: The magnetic force acting on a straight current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is maximum when the angle between current and field is:
e: Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is largest when current flows at 90° (perpendicular) to the magnetic field.

q: Per NCERT, weak ionic currents inside which two human organs produce detectable magnetic fields used in MRI diagnostics?
e: Per NCERT ('Magnetism in Medicine'), tiny ionic nerve/muscle currents in the heart and brain produce weak magnetic fields imaged by MRI.

q: What is the main safety purpose of connecting the metallic body of appliances (toaster, electric iron, refrigerator) to the green earth wire?
o: Provide a low-resistance path for leakage current to keep the casing near zero potential and prevent electric shock
e: Earthing safely diverts leakage currents to Earth so anyone touching the metallic body is protected from electric shock.

q: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit: (NCERT)
e: Direct contact between live and neutral wires drops circuit resistance near zero, causing current to spike heavily.

q: When a bar magnet and a closed coil move at the same speed in the exact same direction (zero relative motion), what is the induced current in the coil?
e: Induced current requires changing magnetic flux due to relative motion; moving together gives zero relative motion and zero current.

q: If the electric current through a long straight wire is doubled, what happens to the strength of the magnetic field at a fixed distance r from the wire?
e: Magnetic field strength around a straight wire is directly proportional to current (B ∝ I), so doubling I doubles B.

q: As you move a magnetic compass farther away (increasing radial distance r) from a current-carrying wire, how does the magnetic field change?
o: Drops to zero right outside the wire
e: Concentric field circles grow wider apart with distance, indicating a weaker magnetic field (B ∝ 1/r).

q: If a circular current-carrying coil has n closely wound turns, how does the magnetic field at its centre compare to a single circular loop with the same current? (NCERT)
o: n times stronger (because fields of all turns add up in the same direction)
e: Current circulates identically in every turn, so individual magnetic fields reinforce linearly to give n times the field.

q: Where around a bar magnet are magnetic field lines closest together (most crowded), and what does this signify?
o: Near the two poles (N and S); strongest magnetic field
e: Crowding of field lines represents field strength; lines are densest near the poles where the magnetic field is strongest.

q: How can the North and South poles of an electromagnet (current-carrying solenoid) be reversed instantaneously?
o: Reversing the direction of electric current by swapping battery terminals
e: Reversing current flow immediately reverses the magnetic polarity of both ends of the solenoid.

q: In what key ways is an electromagnet superior to a permanent bar magnet for industrial applications?
o: Its field strength can be controlled, its polarity reversed, and magnetism switched off at will
It is made from hard steel only
It has only a North pole
e: Electromagnets offer adjustable strength, switchable on/off magnetism, and reversible poles—impossible with permanent magnets.

q: A bar magnet is pushed toward a coil connected to a galvanometer and then held STATIONARY inside the coil. What does the galvanometer needle show while stationary?
o: Returns to zero (no deflection while stationary)
e: Once motion stops, magnetic flux through the coil ceases to change, so induced current immediately drops to zero.

q: Which changes increase the magnetic strength of an electromagnet?
o: Increasing number of coil turns, increasing current, and using a soft iron core
Using AC instead of DC only
e: Strength scales with coil turn density, current magnitude, and insertion of a soft iron core.

q: A positively charged alpha particle enters a uniform magnetic field moving PARALLEL (θ = 0°) to the magnetic field lines. What is the magnetic force on it?
e: Charges or currents moving parallel (0°) or antiparallel (180°) to magnetic field lines experience zero magnetic force.

q: If a neutron (zero electric charge) is projected perpendicular (90°) into a strong uniform magnetic field, what will its trajectory be?
o: Continues straight undeflected (neutral particles experience zero magnetic force)
e: Magnetic force acts only on moving electric charges; being electrically neutral, a neutron travels undeflected.

q: How are commercial electric motors modified to become much more powerful than simple laboratory coil motors?
o: Using iron coil instead of copper
Using an electromagnet instead of a permanent magnet, a large number of turns, and a soft iron armature core
Using a single turn of thick wire
e: Per NCERT, commercial motors employ electromagnets, multi-turn insulated copper coils, and a soft iron core (armature).

q: What is a major advantage of Alternating Current (AC) over Direct Current (DC) for long-distance power distribution?
o: AC voltage can be easily stepped up/down using transformers, transmitting power over long distances with minimal energy loss
AC is easily stored in dry cells
e: AC voltages are readily stepped up and down via transformers to transmit electricity afar with minimal resistive heat loss.

q: In NCERT Activity 13.9 (two coils wound on a paper cylinder): after switching ON the battery in Coil-1 and keeping steady current flowing, what does Coil-2's galvanometer show?
o: A momentary kick only when switching ON (and opposite kick at OFF), returning to ZERO during steady current
e: Mutual induction occurs only while current (and flux) changes—momentarily at switch-on and switch-off, zero during steady DC.

q: Pushing a magnet's North pole quickly INTO a coil deflects a galvanometer needle to the right. Which way will the needle deflect when pulling the SAME North pole quickly OUT?
e: Reversing the direction of magnet motion reverses the polarity of the induced current.

q: What primarily causes electrical short-circuiting in domestic appliances or wiring?
o: Damaged insulation or fault bringing the live wire and neutral wire into direct contact
e: Short-circuiting happens when damaged insulation allows live and neutral wires to touch directly.

q: Which condition can trigger electrical overloading in a household circuit?
o: Accidental hike in supply voltage or connecting too many high-power appliances to a single socket
e: Overloading occurs when current exceeds wire rating—due to supply voltage surges or plugging too many appliances into one socket.

q: Which modern resettable automatic switch is now widely used in place of traditional melt-type fuses in homes?
e: An MCB trips automatically during overcurrent/short-circuit and can be manually reset once the fault is cleared.

q: In an electromagnetic induction experiment, if you move a magnet toward a coil twice as fast, what happens to the induced current?
e: Induced EMF/current increases with the rate at which magnetic flux through the coil changes.

q: Upon which effect of electric current does an ordinary safety fuse work?
o: Heating effect of electric current (Joule heating)
e: A fuse relies on Joule heating (I²Rt): overcurrent raises heat enough to melt the low-melting-point wire.

q: All domestic ON/OFF switches must be connected in which wire, and why?
o: Live wire, so turning the switch OFF completely disconnects the appliance from the dangerous 220 V live potential
e: If switched on the neutral side, the appliance remains at 220 V live potential even when turned off—creating a severe shock hazard.

q: When iron filings are sprinkled around a bar magnet on cardboard and tapped gently, why do they align in curved patterns?
o: The magnet creates a magnetic field that turns each iron filing into a tiny dipole aligning along the field lines
e: Each filing becomes magnetised and aligns along the net magnetic field direction, tracing field lines.

q: Why does a freely pivoted compass needle always align roughly North–South away from magnets, yet deflects sharply near a bar magnet?
o: It is itself a small magnet aligning with Earth's field, easily overridden by the much stronger local field of a nearby bar magnet
e: A compass needle is a tiny pivoted magnet; a nearby bar magnet exerts a much stronger local torque than Earth's weak field.

q: What is the direction of magnetic field lines inside the plane of a circular loop carrying current in the clockwise direction (as viewed from the front)?
o: Out of the page towards the viewer
Perpendicularly INTO the page away from the viewer (behaving as a South pole)
e: Clockwise current creates a South face on the front side, meaning field lines point into the loop (into the page).

q: How can the direction of rotation of a DC electric motor's shaft be reversed?
o: By reversing EITHER the battery polarity (current) OR the magnet's polarity (not both together)
By reversing both current and magnetic poles simultaneously
e: Reversing either current or magnetic field flips the direction of force; flipping both cancels out and keeps rotation the same.

q: In NCERT Activity 13.7, a current-carrying aluminium rod AB suspended between the poles of a horseshoe magnet gets displaced. When is its displacement largest?
o: When the rod lies parallel to the magnetic field
When the direction of current is at right angles (90°) to the direction of the magnetic field
e: Displacement and magnetic force reach maximum when the current-carrying rod is oriented at 90° to the magnetic field.

q: Why are two separate parallel ratings (5 A and 15 A) provided after the electricity meter on the domestic distribution board?
o: 5 A provides DC and 15 A provides AC
5 A circuit powers low-wattage bulbs/fans while 15 A handles heavy-current geysers, ACs, and irons
e: Per NCERT, homes use two circuits: 15 A for high-power appliances (geysers, air coolers) and 5 A for bulbs and fans.

q: Which of the following statements about magnetic field lines is FALSE?
o: They start at the North pole and terminate permanently at the South pole with nothing inside the magnet
e: Unlike electrostatic field lines, magnetic field lines do NOT terminate at poles; they continue S to N inside the magnet as closed loops.

q: Which statement accurately contrasts AC from DC regarding time variation?
o: Direct current (DC) always flows in one direction, whereas alternating current (AC) reverses direction periodically
e: DC maintains constant polarity/direction, whereas AC periodically reverses its direction.

q: By the Right-Hand Thumb Rule, if electric current flows straight AWAY from you (into the plane of your notebook), what is the sense of magnetic field circles?
e: Pointing your right thumb INTO the page causes curled fingers to sweep clockwise.

q: Electric bells, loudspeakers, magnetic cranes, and electric motors all rely essentially on:
o: The magnetic effect of electric current (electromagnetism / magnetic force)
e: All of these devices harness the magnetic fields and forces produced by electric currents.

q: A positively charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards West is deflected towards North by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is: (NCERT)
e: Positive alpha moving West gives current West (middle finger); force North (thumb) => Fleming's Left-Hand Rule puts forefinger (field) UPWARDS.

q: Imagine you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of the magnetic field? (NCERT)
e: Electrons move back-to-front so conventional current runs front-to-back (towards you); Force = Right => Fleming's LHR gives Field vertically DOWNWARDS.

q: A current through a horizontal power line flows in East to West direction. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly BELOW it and directly ABOVE it? (NCERT Ex 13.1)
e: Applying Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule with thumb pointing West, field lines sweep South below the wire and North above it.

q: A vertical wire carries electric current vertically UPWARDS. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point due NORTH of the wire?
e: Right thumb UP makes field lines run anticlockwise (from above: E→N→W→S); at the point due North, the tangent points WEST.

q: An electron travels horizontally towards EAST in a magnetic field directed vertically UPWARDS. What is the direction of magnetic force on the electron?
e: Electron going East means current flows West (middle finger); Field = Up (forefinger) => Fleming's LHR puts Force (thumb) towards NORTH.

q: A horizontal wire carries current from South to North in a uniform magnetic field directed vertically UPWARDS. In which direction will the wire experience a force?
e: Current North (middle finger), Field Up (forefinger) => Fleming's Left-Hand Rule gives Force (thumb) towards EAST.

q: An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a 220 V domestic circuit with a 5 A fuse. What result is expected? (NCERT)
o: Oven draws I = 2000/220 ≈ 9.09 A (> 5 A), causing overloading and melting the fuse
e: I = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.09 A, exceeding the 5 A fuse rating and blowing it.

q: Looking end-on at a current-carrying solenoid AB, the current flows CLOCKWISE at end A and ANTICLOCKWISE at end B. Identify the magnetic poles at A and B.
e: By Clock Face Rule: Clockwise face acts as South pole (A = S), and anticlockwise face acts as North pole (B = N).

q: If the positive and negative battery leads connected to a simple DC motor are swapped, how does its rotation change?
o: Motor reverses its direction of rotation
e: Reversing current while keeping magnet poles fixed reverses magnetic force on the armature, reversing rotation.

q: How does the electrical output of a DC generator differ graphically from that of an AC generator?
o: AC stays one-sided while DC alternates
AC reverses polarity periodically (+ and -), whereas DC stays unidirectional without reversing polarity
e: The split-ring commutator swaps coil connections to external brushes every half turn so DC output keeps a single polarity.

q: An AC generator's armature completes 50 revolutions every second. What are the frequency and time period of the induced AC?
e: Frequency f = 50 Hz; time period T = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.02 s (direction reverses every T/2 = 0.01 s).

q: When moving a magnet back and forth along the axis of a closed coil connected to a galvanometer, when is the galvanometer deflection zero?
o: At the turning instants when the magnet momentarily stops moving
While passing fastest through the coil centre
e: At the instant motion reverses direction, magnet velocity is momentarily zero, so induced current briefly hits zero.

q: Consider a circular loop of wire lying on a table carrying current CLOCKWISE. Using the right-hand rule, find the magnetic field direction inside and outside the loop on the table. (NCERT)
o: Inside: perpendicularly downwards into the table; Outside: perpendicularly upwards out of the table
e: By the right-hand rule, clockwise current sends field lines perpendicularly INTO the table inside the loop and OUT of the table outside it.

q: A vertical wire carries current straight OUT of the page towards you. Which way does the North needle of a compass placed directly to the RIGHT of the wire point?
o: Towards the top of the page
Towards the bottom of the page
e: Right thumb pointing OUT of the page gives anticlockwise field circles; on the right side of the wire, the tangent points UPWARDS.

q: A domestic 220 V power line is protected by a 15 A fuse. Can TWO 1500 W room heaters be operated safely at the same time on this line?
o: Yes, total current is only 6.8 A
Yes mathematically: total power = 3000 W draws I = 3000/220 ≈ 13.64 A (< 15 A fuse limit), though near maximum load
No, because heaters draw zero current
e: Total power = 3000 W draws I = 3000/220 ≈ 13.64 A, which stays within the 15 A rating.

q: Two circular coils A and B are placed close to each other. If the current in coil A is changed, will some current be induced in coil B? Give reason. (NCERT)
o: No, because they are not physically touching
Yes, changing current in A changes the magnetic field linked with coil B, inducing current in B
Only if coil B has its own battery
Only when current in A stays constant
e: Per NCERT, changing current in coil A varies the magnetic field lines passing through coil B, inducing an electric current in B.

q: A magnet is pushed at speed v into a closed coil (circuit 1) and an identical open/broken coil (circuit 2). How do the two compare?
o: Induced current flows in the closed coil, whereas in the open coil induced EMF appears across the ends with zero current
More current flows in the open coil
e: Electric current requires a closed path; an open coil develops induced potential difference across its gap without current flow.

q: What is the normal potential difference maintained between the Red (live) wire and the Black (neutral) wire in Indian domestic supply?
e: With neutral near 0 V and live at 220 V, the potential difference between them in India is 220 V.

q: Under fault-free normal operating conditions, what is the potential difference between the Neutral (black) wire and Earth (green) wire?
e: Both neutral and earth are referenced to ground potential, so the potential difference between them is nearly 0 V.

q: When a small compass is held near one end of a current-carrying solenoid, the compass's North needle turns directly INWARD towards that end. Which pole is that end of the solenoid?
o: South pole — because opposite poles attract
e: The North pole of the compass needle is attracted towards the solenoid's South pole.

q: An electromagnet lifts 10 iron nails with 2 A current and a soft iron core. If current drops to 0.5 A and the iron core is removed, what happens?
o: Magnetic strength drops drastically and it may fail to lift even a single nail
e: Lowering current and removing the soft iron core sharply weakens the magnetic field.

q: A compass needle shows no deflection near a plastic comb, but deflects strongly when a current-carrying copper wire is held parallel just above it. What does this prove?
o: Electric current produces a magnetic field around the conductor (Oersted's experiment)
e: Copper itself is non-magnetic; only electric current flowing through it produces the deflecting magnetic field.

q: Iron filings form concentric circles around a vertical wire passing through cardboard. If the direction of the SAME current is reversed, what happens to the concentric circular pattern?
o: The concentric circular pattern remains identical, though the field direction (compass orientation) reverses
e: Reversing current reverses magnetic field orientation (compass flips 180°), while the geometric concentric-circle pattern stays unchanged.

q: How does a tiny compass needle locate the direction of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet?
o: The direction in which the North pole of the compass needle points gives the magnetic field direction at that point
e: By definition, magnetic field direction at a point is the direction pointed to by the North pole of a compass needle placed there.

q: Compare the magnetic field at a radial distance of 10 cm from a thick copper wire vs a thin copper wire, if BOTH carry the exact same 5 A current.
o: Identical at 10 cm outside both wires (depends on current I and distance r)
e: Outside a straight wire, magnetic field strength depends only on current I and distance r, not the wire's radius.

q: A copper rod sits perpendicular between the poles of a strong magnet, but the circuit switch is kept OPEN (I = 0). What magnetic force acts on the rod?
e: With zero current (I = 0), a stationary non-magnetic copper rod experiences zero magnetic force.

q: A 1.5 kW AC, 1 kW iron, and 1 kW geyser are plugged together into one 15 A socket on a 220 V line. Find total current and outcome.
o: Total 3500 W => I = 3500/220 ≈ 15.9 A (> 15 A), causing overloading and blowing the fuse / tripping MCB
e: Total power = 3500 W gives I = 3500/220 ≈ 15.9 A, exceeding the 15 A rating and triggering overload protection.

q: Why must a blown safety fuse NEVER be replaced by a thick piece of ordinary copper wire?
o: A thick copper wire has a high melting point and current capacity, so it won't melt during faults—risking appliance damage or fire!
e: Thick copper will not melt at fault currents, letting dangerous overcurrent overheat house wiring and cause fires.

q: If a strong magnet lies inside a coil and BOTH move forward together at 10 m/s, will an LED connected to the coil light up?
o: No, because there is zero relative motion and zero change in magnetic flux through the coil
Only while accelerating constantly in opposite frames
e: Zero relative motion means constant flux through the coil—hence zero induced current.

q: In an electric generator, if stronger magnetic poles are used and the coil is rotated faster, how does the output current change?
o: Magnitude of induced current increases substantially
e: Stronger magnetic field and faster rotation both increase the rate of flux linkage change, raising induced current.

q:
Assertion (A): Two magnetic field lines never intersect each other.
Reason (R): If they did, a compass needle placed at the point of intersection would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is impossible.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R is the exact explanation of A.

q:
Assertion (A): The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is uniform at all interior points.
Reason (R): Inside the solenoid, magnetic field lines are parallel and equally spaced straight lines.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains uniformity inside a solenoid.

q:
Assertion (A): Soft iron is preferred for making permanent magnets.
Reason (R): Soft iron is easily magnetised and loses most of its magnetism immediately once the magnetising current is switched off.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (soft iron makes temporary electromagnets, whereas hard steel makes permanent magnets), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Inside a bar magnet, the direction of magnetic field lines is from its South pole to its North pole.
Reason (R): Magnetic field lines always form closed continuous curves.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains why field lines must return from S to N inside the magnet.

q:
Assertion (A): In India, 50 Hz alternating current reverses its direction 50 times per second.
Reason (R): During each complete cycle of alternating current, the direction of flow reverses twice.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (it reverses 50 × 2 = 100 times per second, every 1/100 s), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): A safety fuse is always wired in series with the live wire.
Reason (R): If wired in the neutral wire, a blown fuse would still leave the appliance connected to high 220 V live potential, posing a shock hazard.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains live-wire fuse placement.

q:
Assertion (A): An electron moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field experiences maximum magnetic force.
Reason (R): The magnetic force on a moving charge or current-carrying conductor is zero when motion/current is parallel to the magnetic field lines.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (parallel motion yields zero magnetic force), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): A DC electric motor uses a split-ring commutator.
Reason (R): The split-ring commutator reverses coil current every half rotation so torque keeps turning the armature in one continuous direction.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains commutator action.

q:
Assertion (A): Earthing via the green earth wire is essential for metallic-body appliances like electric irons and geysers.
Reason (R): In case of insulation failure leaking live voltage onto the casing, earthing provides a very low-resistance path to Earth, keeping the casing safe to touch.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains how earthing protects against electric shock.

q:
Assertion (A): Keeping a strong bar magnet stationary inside a closed copper coil generates a steady DC current continuously.
Reason (R): Electromagnetic induction produces current only when magnetic flux linked with the coil changes over time.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (a stationary magnet induces zero current), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): The strength of magnetic field increases as we move further away from a straight current-carrying wire.
Reason (R): Magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (field strength decreases with distance), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Large power-station AC generators use slip rings to deliver current from the rotating armature to the external circuit.
Reason (R): Slip rings swap contact with external carbon brushes every half rotation to deliver unidirectional DC.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is true, while R is false (split rings swap brushes for DC; each slip ring stays permanently in contact with its own brush to yield AC).

q:
Assertion (A): A safety fuse wire is chosen for having high resistance and a very high melting point.
Reason (R): A fuse operates on the heating effect of electric current.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (a fuse must have a LOW melting point, not a high one, so it melts promptly during faults), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Different room branches in domestic electrical circuits are wired in parallel with the mains.
Reason (R): Parallel branches ensure each room gets full 220 V and remains unaffected if one appliance/branch is switched off.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R accurately explains parallel domestic distribution.

q:
Assertion (A): A neutron can pass straight through a strong magnetic field without any deflection.
Reason (R): A magnetic field exerts force only on moving electrically charged particles (when motion is not parallel to the field).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains zero magnetic force on neutral neutrons.

q:
Assertion (A): Moving a bar magnet near a closed coil produces electric current in the coil even without any physical battery or contact.
Reason (R): A changing magnetic field induces electric current inside a closed conducting loop via electromagnetic induction.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains contactless electromagnetic induction.

q:
Assertion (A): During a short circuit, circuit resistance rises sharply to a very high value.
Reason (R): Extremely low resistance causes a massive surge in current that can melt insulation and start fires.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (short circuit drops resistance almost to zero), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): When opposite poles of two bar magnets face each other, field lines emerge from the North pole of one and enter the South pole of the other.
Reason (R): Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines are directed from North pole to South pole.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains the continuous field pattern between facing N and S poles.

q:
Assertion (A): Doubling the number of turns in a circular current-carrying coil doubles the magnetic field at its centre for the same current.
Reason (R): Current flowing in the same sense in each turn makes the magnetic fields of all turns add up constructively.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains why field strength scales with turn count.

q:
Assertion (A): Earthing alone makes a safety fuse unnecessary because earth wire cuts off overload currents.
Reason (R): A fuse disconnects the circuit during excessive current (overloading/short-circuit), whereas earthing safely drains leakage current from metallic bodies to ground.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (fuses handle overcurrent while earthing handles casing leakage—both are essential), while R is true.

q: Case Study: A student wraps 50 turns of insulated copper wire around a soft iron nail and connects a 6 V battery. Closing the switch attracts pins; opening it drops them. What happens if turns are increased from 50 to 150 (at same current)?
o: Magnetic pull strengthens roughly 3 times, lifting noticeably more iron pins
The nail turns into a permanent steel magnet
e: More coil turns linearly strengthen the electromagnet's magnetic field.

q: Case Study: Two coils—Primary (battery + switch) and Secondary (galvanometer)—sit coaxially. If a soft iron rod is inserted through the centres of BOTH coils, how does the momentary galvanometer deflection change at switch-ON/OFF?
o: Soft iron concentrates and amplifies magnetic flux linkage, making momentary ON/OFF deflections much LARGER
e: A soft iron core channels and intensifies magnetic flux between the two coils, magnifying the induced pulse at switch-on/off.

q: Case Study: Inside an electric washing machine, a loose Red wire accidentally touches the metal outer body. Which safety arrangement protects the user touching the metal body?
o: The green Earth wire connected to the metal casing diverts fault current to ground and immediately blows the live fuse / trips the MCB
e: Live-to-casing contact completes a low-resistance path via the green earth wire, surging fault current to trip the live fuse/MCB instantaneously.

q: Case Study: Between horseshoe magnet poles (N bottom, S top => B upwards), a rod carrying current B→A kicks to the LEFT. If BOTH the magnet is inverted (N top, S bottom) AND the battery leads are swapped (A→B), which way will the rod kick now?
o: Still to the LEFT (reversing BOTH magnetic field and current cancels out, leaving force direction unchanged)
e: Reversing both B and I reverses the vector cross-product twice, restoring the exact same LEFT deflection.

q: Case Study: A student replaces a DC motor's split-ring commutator with an unbroken solid slip ring while keeping a DC battery connected. Why does the coil now just oscillate/jam instead of rotating continuously?
o: Without current reversal every 180°, the torque reverses every half turn and rocks the coil back and forth
e: Without split-ring current reversal after half rotation, the coil faces opposite torque and cannot complete continuous unidirectional spin.

q:
Case Study: Match these 3 domestic faults:
1. Plugging heater + geyser + iron into one socket
2. Damaged insulation letting red & black wires touch
3. Leakage current reaching toaster's metal body
Identify the exact match:
e: Excess parallel load causes overloading; live-neutral touch causes short-circuiting; metal body leakage is guarded by earthing.

q: Case Study: An electric iron runs on 50 Hz AC mains. How many times does the alternating current reverse its direction in 1 minute (60 seconds)?
e: 50 Hz reverses twice per cycle = 100 reversals/second. In 60 seconds = 60 × 100 = 6000 reversals!

q: Case Study: Two long parallel wires A and B lie side-by-side and carry heavy DC currents in the EXACT SAME direction. What magnetic interaction occurs between them?
e: Applying RHTR + Fleming's LHR shows parallel wires carrying currents in the SAME direction attract each other.

q: Case Study: While plotting field lines around a bar magnet placed with its N-pole pointing geographical North, two neutral points appear where a compass shows no preferred direction. What happens at a neutral point?
o: The magnet's field and Earth's horizontal magnetic field are equal and opposite, cancelling net field to zero
e: At a neutral point, the magnet's field exactly cancels Earth's horizontal field, leaving net B = 0.

q: Case Study: Two identical 100-turn coils X and Y both carry 2 A DC; X has a wooden/copper core while Y has a soft iron core. Why does Y lift vastly heavier steel weights?
o: Soft iron is ferromagnetic and strongly reinforces the coil's magnetic field by hundreds of times
e: Ferromagnetic soft iron aligns its domains with the solenoid field, amplifying total magnetic flux tremendously.

q: A proton moves horizontally NORTH while an electron moves horizontally SOUTH into the SAME uniform magnetic field directed vertically DOWNWARDS. What are the directions of magnetic forces on the proton and electron respectively?
o: BOTH experience magnetic force towards WEST (since a North-moving proton and South-moving electron both carry conventional current towards NORTH!)
e: Brilliant HOTS trap! Positive proton going North = current North. Negative electron going South = conventional current opposite = ALSO North! With B Downwards, Fleming's LHR pushes BOTH towards WEST!

q: What exact combination of electrical and thermal properties makes a wire ideal as a safety fuse?
o: Low resistivity and high melting point
High resistivity (to heat up quickly via I²Rt) and LOW melting point (to melt promptly)
High resistivity and high melting point
Zero resistance and infinite melting point
e: A fuse needs relatively high resistivity to generate heat rapidly and a low melting point so it melts safely before copper wiring overheats.

q: A wire carrying 10 A sits inside a strong 2 T magnetic field, yet experiences ZERO magnetic force. When is this possible?
o: When the wire is at 90° to the field
When the wire lies parallel (0°) or antiparallel (180°) to the magnetic field lines
When DC is used instead of AC
e: Magnetic force is zero whenever current runs parallel or antiparallel to magnetic field lines (θ = 0° or 180°).

q: Coil-1 and Coil-2 sit coaxially without touching. Steady 5 A current in Coil-1 is smoothly reduced to 0 A over 2 seconds, then kept at 0 A. During which interval does Coil-2 have induced current?
o: Only during the 2-second interval while current was changing from 5 A down to 0 A
e: Induced current appears in Coil-2 strictly during the 2-second window when Coil-1's current and magnetic field are actively changing.

q: A bar magnet is dropped vertically through the centre of a closed horizontal copper ring. Will its downward acceleration be equal to, less than, or greater than g (9.8 m/s²)?
o: Equal to g since copper is non-magnetic
LESS than g (induced current in the copper ring opposes the magnet's fall, conserving energy)
e: Changing flux induces eddy current in the closed copper ring whose magnetic field opposes the falling magnet (Lenz's law), reducing acceleration below g.

q: Now the same bar magnet is dropped vertically through a horizontal copper ring that has a small radial SLIT/CUT in it (making it an open loop). What is the magnet's acceleration now?
o: Equal to g (9.8 m/s²) because the cut opens the loop, preventing induced current and opposing magnetic force
e: With a slit breaking the conducting loop, no induced current can circulate, eliminating the opposing magnetic force so acceleration remains g.

q: If both the armature current AND magnetic field strength in a motor are doubled, by what factor does the magnetic force on the coil conductors increase?
e: Since F = BIl, doubling both B and I multiplies the magnetic force by 2 × 2 = 4 times.

q: An electrician mistakenly installs a wall switch in the Black (neutral) wire instead of the Red (live) wire. With the switch turned OFF, why is touching the ceiling fan's bare internal terminal still fatal?
o: Even with the switch OFF, the appliance remains directly connected to the 220 V live line—touching it completes a circuit to Earth causing electric shock
e: Switching the neutral wire leaves the entire appliance live at 220 V even when off, creating a lethal path through anyone touching it to ground.

q: A bar magnet lies horizontally pointing North–South (North pole towards North). If a tiny compass is placed right beside its midpoint on the EAST side (neglecting Earth's field), which way will the compass's North needle point?
o: South (outside the bar magnet, field lines run from its North end back towards its South end)
e: Outside the magnet, field lines curve back from the North pole (North end) to the South pole (South end), pointing SOUTH alongside its middle.

q: In a solenoid of fixed length, the number of turns is doubled from 200 to 400 while the current is halved from 2 A to 1 A. What happens to the magnetic field inside?
e: Inside a solenoid, field strength scales with ampere-turns per unit length (n·I); doubling turns and halving current leaves n·I unchanged.

q: Electrons revolve CLOCKWISE in a circular loop lying on a horizontal table when viewed from above. What is the direction of the conventional current and the top magnetic pole of the loop?
o: Clockwise current, South pole on top
Anticlockwise conventional current, North pole on top
e: Careful! Clockwise motion of negative electrons equals ANTICLOCKWISE conventional current, making the top face a North pole.

q: A toaster's green earth wire is disconnected, leaving only live (red) and neutral (black) connected. Will the toaster work normally when healthy, and when does the danger strike?
o: Toaster works while intact, but if the live heating element ever touches the metal casing, lacking earthing exposes anyone touching it to 220 V shock
Fuse blows immediately even when healthy
e: During normal operation current flows through live and neutral only; earthing serves specifically as life-saving fault protection if live touches the casing.

q: Both ends X and Y of a metal rod ATTRACT the North pole of a freely suspended bar magnet! What is the only valid scientific conclusion?
o: The rod is a magnet with two South poles
The rod is an unmagnetised magnetic material (such as soft iron), NOT a permanent magnet
The rod is made of copper
The rod has only a North pole
e: Repulsion is the sure test of magnetisation. A rod whose both ends attract the same pole must be an unmagnetised ferromagnetic material like iron.

q: An alpha particle (charge +2e) and a proton (charge +e) enter perpendicular to the same magnetic field with identical speed v. What is the ratio of magnetic forces acting on them (F_α : F_p)?
e: At equal v and B perpendicular to velocity, magnetic force F = qvB is proportional to charge q: (+2e)/(+e) = 2 : 1.

q: If a fuse is wrongly placed only in the NEUTRAL wire and melts during an overload, will the appliance stop running, and is it safe to repair without unplugging?
o: Stops running and is completely safe to touch
The appliance turns off, YET remains dangerously energised at 220 V from the live wire—a severe shock hazard!
e: Opening the neutral line stops current, so the device appears off while still sitting live at 220 V potential.

q: Which description correctly matches the waveform of domestic Indian mains (220 V, 50 Hz)?
o: A sinusoidal wave completing 50 full cycles per second and crossing zero/reversing 100 times per second
e: 50 Hz sinusoidal AC completes 50 positive–negative cycles each second, reversing polarity 100 times/s.

q: If a copper coil is replaced by an identical-shape nichrome coil of 10× higher resistance, and the magnet is pushed at the same speed, how do induced voltage (EMF) and induced current compare?
o: Induced EMF remains the same, while induced current drops to 1/10 due to Ohm's law (I = EMF/R)
e: Induced EMF depends solely on coil turns and rate of flux change, whereas induced current drops inversely with coil resistance (I = EMF/R).

q: A horizontal wire carries current from WEST to EAST. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point due NORTH of the wire in the SAME horizontal plane?
e: Pointing right thumb East (+x), curled fingers point vertically UPWARDS (+z) on the North side of the wire and downwards on the South side.

q: A closed square copper loop ABCD lies inside a vast uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane. If the loop is translated (slid) straight to the right while remaining completely inside the uniform field, what current is induced?
o: ZERO (while moving inside a uniform field without tilting or leaving, total magnetic flux stays constant)
e: With constant field strength, constant loop area, and fixed orientation, magnetic flux never changes—yielding zero induced current.

q: Two identical concentric circular coils carrying equal currents lie perpendicular (90°) to each other, producing equal individual fields B along North and East at their common centre. What is the magnitude of the resultant field at the centre?
e: Magnetic fields add as vectors; two equal orthogonal fields B yield resultant √(B² + B²) = √2 B.

q: Which distinction between Fleming's Left-Hand Rule and Right-Hand Rule is ALWAYS valid?
o: Left-Hand Rule finds Force/Motion when Field & Current are given (Motors); Right-Hand Rule finds Induced Current when Field & Motion are given (Generators)
Both assign electric current to the thumb
e: Both share Thumb=Motion/Force, Forefinger=Field, Middle=Current; Left applies when current causes motion (motor), Right when motion induces current (generator).

q: In a rotating AC generator armature, at what coil orientations relative to the magnetic field lines is the induced current MAXIMUM versus ZERO?
o: Maximum when coil plane is perpendicular to field
MAXIMUM when coil plane is parallel to the field lines (arms cut lines perpendicularly), and ZERO when coil plane is perpendicular to the field
e: When the coil plane lies parallel to field lines, its moving sides cut across field lines perpendicularly—giving maximum induced current.

q: If a single bar magnet is broken cleanly across its middle into two equal halves, what happens to the magnetic poles of each half?
o: One piece becomes a pure North monopole and the other pure South
Each piece becomes a complete independent magnet possessing BOTH a North and a South pole
e: Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist; breaking a magnet always creates new N–S pairs on every fragment.

q: Why do heavy-inductance motors or transformers often produce a noticeable electrical spark right at the switch contacts when switched OFF rather than when gently running?
o: Rapid collapse of current at switch-off causes a sudden rapid change in magnetic field, inducing high back-voltage across the opening gap
Because copper melts at room temperature
e: Abrupt current interruption causes rapid magnetic field collapse, inducing a momentary high voltage spike across the opening contacts.

q: In a 220 V branch circuit fitted with a 2 A fuse, five 60 W bulbs operate in parallel. Someone then plugs a 1000 W heater into the same branch. Compare the total current before and after.
o: Before: 1.36 A (safe); After: ≈ 5.91 A => 2 A fuse blows immediately!
e: Five 60 W bulbs draw 300/220 ≈ 1.36 A (safe under 2 A). Adding 1000 W raises total to 1300/220 ≈ 5.91 A, immediately blowing the 2 A fuse.

q:
Evaluate these 3 statements:
1. A freely suspended current-carrying solenoid aligns in the North–South direction like a bar magnet.
2. Magnetic fields act inside electric motors.
3. All three domestic wires (Red, Black, Green) always carry 220 V.
Which are TRUE?
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true; statement 3 is false because only the Red live wire is at 220 V while neutral and earth stay near 0 V.

q:
Match each rule with its exact application:
A. Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule
B. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
C. Fleming's Right-Hand Rule
Applications: (i) Induced current direction, (ii) Magnetic field around straight wire, (iii) Force on current-carrying conductor
e: Thumb rule -> magnetic field around wire (ii); Left-hand rule -> force on conductor (iii); Right-hand rule -> induced current (i).

q: Why does the North-seeking pole of a freely suspended compass needle point towards Earth's geographic North?
o: Earth's internal geodynamo acts as if a magnetic SOUTH pole lies near geographic North, attracting the compass needle's North pole
e: Opposite poles attract; hence the compass's North pole points towards the magnetic South pole located near Earth's geographic North.

q: Why are iron armature cores in real electric motors and generators built from thin laminated sheets rather than one solid block of iron?
o: Laminated sheets break up unwanted swirling induced currents (eddy currents) inside the iron core that would otherwise waste energy as heat
e: Varying magnetic fields induce circulating eddy currents inside solid metal cores; insulated laminations curb these heat losses.

q: A home's 15 A main MCB trips instantly whenever a room cooler is switched ON, even though all other heavy loads are OFF. What is the most likely electrical fault?
o: An internal short circuit or severe earth fault inside the cooler draws massive fault current (> 15 A), tripping the MCB
e: A healthy cooler draws around 1–2 A; instant 15 A MCB tripping indicates an internal short circuit or earth fault.
